title: 639. The Leader Who Talks Most Gets Heard Least
author: Business Leader Daily
summary: This Business Leader Daily issue argues that most leaders talk too much, mistaking more words for more clarity. It points out that teams are already buried in email and meetings, so every extra paragraph forces them to search for the one part that matters, and cites a Grammarly and Harris Poll estimate that poor communication costs US businesses up to 1.2 trillion dollars a year. The writer's thesis is that length signals unfinished thinking, because the leader has not made the hard call about what matters most. The advice is to write down the one thing people must take away, to cut until it hurts, and to drop jargon. A second move is repetition, using the same idea in the same language across meetings and updates until the team can repeat it. The issue closes with a Keep Learning list of quotes from Carmine Gallo, Todd Rogers, Nancy Duarte, Chip Heath and others on brevity and clear communication. It is a brief piece, but its rule of one sentence, then repeat, is easy to apply.
points: Rambling usually signals unfinished thinking, since the leader has left the listener to sort out what matters most.
Before sending or speaking, write the single takeaway in one sentence; if that is not possible, the message is not ready.
Cutting jargon and extra paragraphs respects a team that is already overloaded with messages.
A sharp message delivered once disappears, so repeat the same idea in the same words across meetings and updates until the team can finish your sentences.
The curse of knowledge makes leaders overestimate how clear their explanation is, which makes brevity and repetition necessary.
quotes: They mistake more words for more clarity. They think a longer explanation proves a greater understanding.
Your team is already buried. The inbox is overflowing and the calendar is full. Every extra paragraph you send makes them search harder for the one part that matters.
When a leader rambles, the thinking usually isn’t done. Nobody has made the hard call about what matters most. Everything gets said, and the listener is left to sort it out.
Before you hit send or walk into the all-hands, write down the one thing people need to walk away with. If you can’t say it in a sentence, you aren’t ready to say it yet.
A sharp message delivered once is gone before you leave the room. Pick your words and stick with them.
Same idea, same language, in every meeting and every update, until your team can finish your sentences for you.
The Curse of Knowledge: when we are given knowledge, it is impossible to imagine what it's like to LACK that knowledge.
